title: London

jokes.text: I warned you about this. Standard birth control methods aren't usually effective against a Swanson.
jokes.setup: Ron is told Diane is pregnant and says 'We were so careful.'
jokes.punchline: Ron deadpans that standard birth control isn't effective 'against a Swanson,' implying his virility is a force of nature beyond medical science.
jokes.explanation: This is a masterclass in character comedy. Only Ron Swanson could deliver this line with complete sincerity. It simultaneously plays on his hyper-masculine mythology, his deadpan delivery, and the absurdist premise that his genetics are literally superhuman. The economy is perfect — one sentence establishes the entire comic worldview. Earns its high score because it's built entirely from character, not a cheap shortcut.

dialogue.speaker: Diane
dialogue.line: Ron, can we talk in private?

dialogue.speaker: Diane's father
dialogue.line: Of course, sweetheart.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: I think she means me.

jokes.text: I was going to wait until our anniversary, and take you somewhere romantic, perhaps in a canoe. Most likely in a canoe. I actually built a canoe for that purpose.
jokes.setup: Ron is about to propose, explaining he had a romantic plan.
jokes.punchline: The escalating specificity — 'perhaps a canoe,' 'most likely a canoe,' 'I actually built a canoe for that purpose' — reveals Ron's idea of romance is entirely Ron-flavored.
jokes.explanation: The triple escalation of canoe specificity is beautifully structured. 'Perhaps' → 'most likely' → 'I actually built one' is a perfect comedic three-beat. The joke is entirely earned through six seasons of established Ron Swanson character. He's a man who builds things; of course he built a canoe for a marriage proposal. High marks for structure and character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: I have the fertility of a biblical patriarch and the virility of a 1970s porn star. Condoms are a suggestion. Birth control is merely a courteous heads-up.

jokes.text: The fourth floor. Getting married. / Okee dokee. Well, catch you later. / What? Why?
jokes.setup: Ron casually announces he's going upstairs to get married right now.
jokes.punchline: Leslie's brain short-circuits. She says 'Okee dokee, catch you later' on autopilot before the information registers, then freezes.
jokes.explanation: A beautifully constructed reaction beat. Leslie's automatic 'okee dokee, catch you later' followed by a delayed-reaction 'what? why?' perfectly captures how the human brain processes shocking news — autopilot first, comprehension second. The economy is extraordinary: three short lines carry an enormous comedic payload.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: I'm taking Diane somewhere romantic. Perhaps in a canoe.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: Most likely in a canoe.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: I've already built the canoe.

jokes.text: Are you dead? You look like you're in rictus. / I just, I'm having so many thoughts and feelings that I'm paralyzed right now.
jokes.setup: Leslie has processed that Ron is getting married right now and is visually frozen.
jokes.punchline: Ann's clinical medical description — 'rictus' — applied to Leslie's emotional paralysis, followed by Leslie's helpless explanation.
jokes.explanation: Ann using 'rictus' — a medical/clinical term for the grimace of a corpse — to describe Leslie's frozen face is a great character-specific choice. The joke works on two levels: visual (we can picture Leslie's face) and character (Ann as a nurse going clinical). Strong character integration for both characters.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: I'll give you anything in the world.

dialogue.speaker: Diane
dialogue.line: Just promise me one thing: no big, elaborate proposal. I don't want any of that.

jokes.text: Ron is getting married, and I love him, and I care about him, and this is the greatest day ever, and I do not have time to talk about this.
jokes.setup: Leslie is trying to process the marriage news while running after Ron.
jokes.punchline: The stream-of-consciousness confession of love and happiness immediately undercut by 'I do not have time to talk about this' — Leslie's emotions and her action-orientation in perfect collision.
jokes.explanation: This captures Leslie perfectly — she's simultaneously the most emotionally expressive person in any room and the most task-oriented. The contradiction within one breath is the entire Leslie Knope character in microcosm.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: My idea of simple is literally going upstairs in the government building.

jokes.text: Wait! If you would just slow down a little, then I could arrange balloons or a flower cake or a bouncy castle or some...
jokes.setup: Ron is walking purposefully to get married with zero ceremony.
jokes.punchline: Leslie's escalating list of wedding decorations — 'balloons,' 'flower cake,' 'bouncy castle' — goes increasingly absurd as her sentence gets cut off, suggesting she had even wilder ideas.
jokes.explanation: The escalation from 'balloons' to 'bouncy castle' in a wedding context is well-structured, and the cut-off sentence implies even more absurdity. Strong character integration — Leslie planning a wedding on the spot is peak Leslie.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: We've been working on the most important project in Pawnee history. We're fixing a pothole on Ramsett Park Road.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I know what you're thinking: 'Leslie, a pothole? That's not important.' But you're wrong. This pothole is a symbol of everything that's broken in our city. And when we fix it, we're not just filling asphalt. We're filling the hole in Pawnee's heart.

jokes.text: Diane Tammy Lewis. / Tammy? Your middle name is... / Just kidding. It's Elizabeth.
jokes.setup: The officiant asks for full names. Diane gives hers and reveals her middle name is 'Tammy.'
jokes.punchline: Given Ron's two ex-wives named Tammy (a major running gag of the series), this is a gut-punch followed by relief — it was a joke. The callback to the Tammy mythology is perfectly timed.
jokes.explanation: This is the episode's best constructed joke. It weaponizes the entire Tammy mythology built over multiple seasons for a single devastating misdirect. Ron's unspoken horror is the setup; Diane's quick 'just kidding' is the release. The economy is extraordinary — it's delivered in under five seconds and earns maximum impact. Diane proves she's Ron's match by pranking him with his deepest fear at the altar. Rewatch value is high because you can see it coming the second time and anticipate Ron's reaction.

dialogue.speaker: Diane
dialogue.line: Is she okay? Her mouth is just... frozen like that.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: That's a rictus. It's a medical term for when the facial muscles contract involuntarily.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I'm fine! I'm great! This is just my face now.

jokes.text: This is like a waking nightmare of happiness.
jokes.setup: Leslie is overwhelmed with joy at the impromptu wedding.
jokes.punchline: The oxymoron 'waking nightmare of happiness' perfectly captures Leslie's emotional overload — she's so happy it's become distressing.
jokes.explanation: Five words that perfectly encapsulate a feeling everyone has had but nobody has ever named this well. The phrase is original, perfectly economical, deeply character-specific (only Leslie could be distressed by happiness), and immediately quotable. One of the episode's most memorable lines. Comparable in quality to the 8.0 anchor — sharp, unexpected, highly quotable, perfect economy.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Ron's getting married! I'm so happy I could—

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: No. Not doing this.

jokes.text: Why don't you hold this colorful bouquet of highlighters?
jokes.setup: Leslie needs a bouquet for the wedding but there are none in City Hall.
jokes.punchline: Ben produces a bunch of colorful highlighters as a wedding bouquet substitute — practical, absurd, and weirdly touching.
jokes.explanation: A lovely visual gag that balances absurdism with genuine sweetness. The specificity — colorful highlighters as a bouquet — is both funny and fitting for a City Hall wedding. Good character-appropriate improvisation from Ben.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I'm so happy but also so stressed. This is like a nightmare of happiness!

jokes.text: Rice, I need to find some rice. I need to throw some rice. Why is there no rice in this municipal government building?
jokes.setup: The impromptu wedding is moving forward and Leslie is frantically trying to make it traditional.
jokes.punchline: The escalating absurdity of Leslie demanding rice in a government building, culminating in the genuine indignation of 'why is there no rice in this municipal government building?' as if this is a reasonable expectation.
jokes.explanation: Leslie's righteous indignation about the absence of rice in a government building is perfectly absurd. The joke works because she's entirely sincere — she genuinely expected to find rice somehow.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Okay, we can use office supplies! Ben, look at this bouquet I made from a stapler, some file folders, and a three-hole punch!

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Leslie, that's...

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Beautiful? I know! And the centerpieces can be made from highlighters and binder clips!

jokes.text: Haven't I done a quickie wedding for you before? / It's certainly possible, but this one's going to stick.
jokes.setup: The officiant vaguely recognizes Ron from a previous impromptu wedding.
jokes.punchline: Ron's 'it's certainly possible' acknowledges his multiple failed marriages with total equanimity, and 'this one's going to stick' is delivered with Ron's characteristic unshakeable confidence.
jokes.explanation: Two beautifully constructed lines. 'It's certainly possible' — acknowledging he's been married so many times he can't track all his City Hall ceremonies — is a devastating character observation delivered with zero self-pity. 'This one's going to stick' carries real warmth and conviction. Excellent economy and character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: We need to find champagne flutes, napkins with a monogram, and a runner for the aisle. Where would a government building keep those?

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Leslie, this is a Parks Department. We have a broom closet and a lost and found that smells like sadness.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Well, we're going to make it work. Jerry, do we have anything fancy in storage?

dialogue.speaker: Jerry
dialogue.line: We have some folding chairs from 1987 and a broken projector.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Perfect! We'll spray paint them.

jokes.text: Ooh, it's gonna start! / Oh, it's happening. / Oh, my God. / She said yes. / Okay.
jokes.setup: The officiant begins the ceremony vows.
jokes.punchline: Leslie provides running commentary on the wedding ceremony as if she's watching a sporting event — audible gasps and color commentary for each line of the standard vows.
jokes.explanation: Leslie's sportscaster-style commentary on a wedding ceremony she's attending in real-time is a perfect comedic bit. Her inability to contain herself even while participating is pure Leslie. The escalating mini-reactions build beautifully.

dialogue.speaker: Ron Swanson
dialogue.line: I want to get married immediately.

dialogue.speaker: Justice of the Peace
dialogue.line: Ron? Ron Swanson? Haven't I married you before?

dialogue.speaker: Ron Swanson
dialogue.line: Twice. Maybe three times.

dialogue.speaker: Justice of the Peace
dialogue.line: This is my fifth time marrying you.

jokes.text: Wait! Before you, Carl, just one second. I would just like to give a short speech. If I may. / You have 10 seconds.
jokes.setup: Leslie interrupts the officiant to give a speech at the last possible second.
jokes.punchline: Ron flatly gives her '10 seconds,' a perfect encapsulation of their friendship — he knows she needs to say something, and he's giving her exactly as little room as possible.
jokes.explanation: A great two-character joke. Ron's '10 seconds' is an entire relationship distilled into two words — he knows Leslie, accommodates her just enough, and tolerates zero excess. His line has enormous craft economy.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: What's your full name for the license?

dialogue.speaker: Diane
dialogue.line: Diane Tammy Lewis.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: Did you just say Tammy?

jokes.text: At first glance, it may seem as though Ron Swanson and I have nothing in common. But Webster's Dictionary defines 'friend'... / Time.
jokes.setup: Leslie begins a wedding speech using the most clichéd speech-opening imaginable ('Webster's Dictionary defines...')
jokes.punchline: Ron cuts her off at exactly 10 seconds — 'Time.' — which is perfectly timed and also mercifully interrupts what would have been a terrible speech opening.
jokes.explanation: A perfectly constructed two-beat joke. The setup is the meta-comedy of Leslie beginning with 'Webster's Dictionary defines...' — a cliché so worn it's become the go-to parody of bad speeches. The callback payoff — Ron saying 'Time' at exactly the right moment — is both a callback to his 10-second limit and a rescue from Leslie's worst instincts. Ron's single-word response does enormous comedic work. This is excellent craft.

dialogue.speaker: Ron Swanson
dialogue.line: It's Tammy.

dialogue.speaker: Multiple
dialogue.line: [Gasps and panic from the group]

dialogue.speaker: Ron Swanson
dialogue.line: Tammy Two.

dialogue.speaker: Multiple
dialogue.line: [Collective sigh of relief]

jokes.text: I could tell where you were going with that, and it was going to be beautiful.
jokes.setup: Ron cuts Leslie's speech off at 10 seconds after she opens with 'Webster's Dictionary defines...'
jokes.punchline: Ron sincerely (and wrongly) believes what she was building toward would have been beautiful — his affection for her overrides his objectivity about her speech quality.
jokes.explanation: The sweetest joke in the wedding sequence. Ron, who just cut her off from what was obviously going to be a terrible speech, genuinely believes it would have been beautiful. It's simultaneously funny (he's wrong) and deeply moving (he loves Leslie). The deadpan delivery of this line is what makes it land — any warmth in the delivery would undercut it.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: It was the best of times, it was the worst of times. Actually, you know what? I'm just going to wing it from here.

jokes.text: The reception will be held in each of our individual houses, alone.
jokes.setup: The wedding is concluded with everyone celebrating.
jokes.punchline: Ron's idea of a reception is everyone going home separately — the most anti-social possible response to a wedding celebration.
jokes.explanation: A perfect Ron Swanson joke. The specific phrasing 'in each of our individual houses, alone' is hilarious — he doesn't just say 'go home,' he specifies the separateness and the solitude. This is the platonic ideal of character comedy: only Ron Swanson could say this line. High quotability.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: I've decided to skip the reception. I'll be in my office if anyone needs me.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Ron, it's your wedding reception.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: Exactly. Which is why I need to get away from all these people.

jokes.text: Pretend this is rice. [Leslie throws highlighters at the departing couple]
jokes.setup: Leslie was unable to find rice for the wedding.
jokes.punchline: She throws her bouquet-highlighters after Ron and Diane as they leave, narrating 'pretend this is rice' — the callback to her earlier rice hunt, now visually resolved with office supplies.
jokes.explanation: A beautifully economical visual callback that resolves two earlier setups (the rice search and the highlighter bouquet) in a single moment. The instruction 'pretend this is rice' delivered to no one in particular is very funny. A tight, well-constructed button to the wedding sequence.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I couldn't find any rice, so I'm using quinoa instead!

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Leslie, that's a hundred dollars worth of quinoa.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: It's biodegradable and gluten-free. You're welcome.

jokes.text: Last week, I was an answer in the Pawnee Journal's crossword puzzle. The clue? 'Who's the worst?'
jokes.setup: Leslie is describing the severity of the recall campaign against her.
jokes.punchline: Being a crossword answer for 'Who's the worst?' is a specific, creative, and devastating detail that escalates her victimhood in a uniquely Pawnee way.
jokes.explanation: A very specific and original detail — the crossword clue is the perfect specificity to make this land. 'Who's the worst?' as a crossword clue implies whoever wrote that puzzle really committed to the bit. The specificity of journalism weaponized against Leslie in this particular way is inventive and well-structured.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Being reduced to a crossword answer with a brutal clue

jokes.text: There are slugs everywhere on the sidewalk in front of my house. I want them gone. But not killed. I love animals. But get rid of them. They're gross. But make sure they're happy. But not too happy.
jokes.setup: Leslie is doing her 'No Problem Too Small' initiative, hearing citizen complaints.
jokes.punchline: Gretel's series of contradictory demands — remove the slugs but don't kill them, they're gross but make sure they're happy but not too happy — is an escalating absurdist portrait of an impossible constituent.
jokes.explanation: The escalating self-contradiction structure is perfectly executed — each 'but' undercuts the previous demand until the final 'but not too happy' becomes genuinely absurdist. Good structure and escalation.

dialogue.speaker: Gretel
dialogue.line: Remove all the slugs, but don't kill them. And make them happy.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: How am I supposed to make a slug happy?

dialogue.speaker: Gretel
dialogue.line: That's not my problem. Oh, and one more thing — they have to be gone by tomorrow.

jokes.text: Well, as a wise woman once said to me, 'Ann, you cunning, pliable, chestnut-haired sunfish, phase 26 is the key to my plan.'
jokes.setup: Ann is checking in on Leslie's recall fight strategy.
jokes.punchline: Ann quotes Leslie's elaborate, affectionate, absurd compliment-names back to her — revealing Leslie calls her these things all the time and that 'sunfish' is apparently a compliment.
jokes.explanation: A great callback to Leslie's nickname habit. 'Cunning, pliable, chestnut-haired sunfish' is a magnificent nonsense compliment. The fact that Ann has memorized it and delivers it word-perfect suggests this is routine. Good quotability for the nickname itself.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Ann, you're like an oasis of presence in a desert of absence. Your nose is really weird though.

jokes.text: Boy, oh boy, we live interesting lives, filled with unexpected challenges. Life is precious and every day is a miracle.
jokes.setup: The slug infestation has just been mentioned as the most petty possible civic complaint.
jokes.punchline: Chris responds to a slug problem with the profound enthusiasm of a man who has truly convinced himself everything is meaningful — applying maximum life-philosophy to minimum stakes.
jokes.explanation: A solid Chris Traeger joke — his compulsive positivity applied to trivial situations is his core comic register. The juxtaposition of 'life is precious' with slug complaints is good but not his best version of this joke.

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: We spent like twenty minutes talking about slugs.

dialogue.speaker: Chris
dialogue.line: Slugs are just snails that have evolved past the need for a shell. They're like the free spirits of the mollusk world. That's beautiful.

jokes.text: What a freak. / Things with me and Chris are going really well.
jokes.setup: Ann just witnessed Chris's over-the-top philosophical response to slug news.
jokes.punchline: Ann's talking-head immediately following: she calls him 'a freak' then pivots to 'Things with me and Chris are going really well' — the juxtaposition is the joke.
jokes.explanation: A perfectly structured cut-away joke. The whiplash between 'what a freak' and 'things with me and Chris are going really well' is timed perfectly. The mockumentary format enables this construction brilliantly — the camera catches her unguarded and then she performs normalcy.

dialogue.speaker: Chris
dialogue.line: Ann, I just realized we're out of regular coffee. We only have decaf.

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: Chris, you're insane.

jokes.text: And check this out. [holds up hand] / Oh, no, there's no ring. We just had manicures together recently. / Sorry, that was misleading.
jokes.setup: Ann says she and Chris are going really well and says 'check this out' while raising her hand.
jokes.punchline: She pre-emptively clarifies there's no engagement ring — she just got a manicure — but the misdirection was clearly intentional. Her apology 'that was misleading' acknowledges she played the audience.
jokes.explanation: A well-constructed talking-head misdirect. The three-beat structure (tease, reveal, acknowledgment) is clean. 'Sorry, that was misleading' is a funny meta-confession of having baited the audience.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: They copied my store exactly. My exact store!

dialogue.speaker: Lawyer
dialogue.line: Well, Mr. Haverford, think of it this way. If I baked a chocolate chip cookie, and you baked the exact same chocolate chip cookie, my cookie would still be the original.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Right, right.

dialogue.speaker: Lawyer
dialogue.line: But if your cookie was better, and more people wanted your cookie, then your cookie would be the successful cookie. But it would still be a copy.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: So... what you're saying is my cookie is better?

jokes.text: You see, you are Hydrox, Mr. Haverford. We are Oreo.
jokes.setup: The mysterious competitor has opened a store identical to Tom's Rent A Swag directly across the street.
jokes.punchline: The lawyer calls Tom's store 'Hydrox' — the inferior knockoff cookie brand — while declaring their client 'Oreo,' implying Tom is the cheap imitation even of his own original concept.
jokes.explanation: A genuinely clever analogy — Hydrox was in fact the original chocolate sandwich cookie (predating Oreo) but is universally perceived as the knockoff. The irony that Tom IS the original but gets called Hydrox is sharp. Good cultural specificity.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: How did he even get here? Does he have a helicopter? A private jet?

dialogue.speaker: Lawyer
dialogue.line: It wasn't Vin Diesel.

jokes.text: My client is not Jason Statham. If that's what you're thinking.
jokes.setup: Tom speculates about who the mysterious competitor's 'transporter' might be.
jokes.punchline: The lawyer specifically denies it's Jason Statham — which no one said, making the denial feel oddly specific and therefore suspicious.
jokes.explanation: A well-executed absurdist non-denial denial. The humor comes from the specificity of the disclaimer — by naming Statham, the lawyer inadvertently suggests the thought. The joke plays on the 'Transporter' film franchise cleverly.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Where do you think they keep all the NBA trophies? Like, in a vault somewhere?

dialogue.speaker: Lawyer
dialogue.line: I don't know, Tom. Why would I know that?

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: I'm just saying, if I were an NBA trophy, I'd want to be somewhere safe and climate-controlled.

dialogue.speaker: Lawyer
dialogue.line: That's... not how trophies work.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Look, I'm not saying LeBron James is stealing them. I'm just saying he has the means and the motive.

dialogue.speaker: Lawyer
dialogue.line: He doesn't have either of those things.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Well, LeBron, if you're listening, I didn't say that.

jokes.text: I'm sure this guy is just looking for a place to store all his NBA Championship trophies. / It's not LeBron James. / Damn.
jokes.setup: Tom guesses at the identity of the mysterious competitor.
jokes.punchline: The lawyer's pre-emptive denial of LeBron James mirrors the Statham denial — establishing a running bit of specific non-denials — while Tom's 'damn' is perfect defeated acceptance.
jokes.explanation: The callback to the Statham denial structure works well. Tom's 'Damn' — genuinely disappointed — is the real punchline. The running gag of specific celebrity non-denials is a nice structural choice.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: I just had a brilliant idea.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: We should get lunch.

jokes.text: Think Outside of the Box? / Of course. It was an amazing phase. / Easily a top-five phase.
jokes.setup: Ben references 'Phase 13' of Leslie's 40-phase defense strategy.
jokes.punchline: The characters treat a list of phases in an internal political strategy as if they're debating classic albums — 'amazing phase,' 'top-five phase' — the grandiosity applied to bureaucratic process planning.
jokes.explanation: The joke is in the reverence — treating government strategy phases like a greatest-hits countdown. It's a gentle poke at Leslie's bureaucratic grandeur. Functional and character-specific.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: Leslie, you won an award.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Oh my god, really? Wait, are you messing with me? Because if this is a prank, it's not funny.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: No, you actually won it.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Oh. Well then it's the best day of my life.

jokes.text: Oh, my God, this is real. I just assumed you were lying.
jokes.setup: April tells Leslie she nominated her for an international women in government award.
jokes.punchline: Leslie's immediate assumption was that April was lying — which tells us everything about April's character and their relationship.
jokes.explanation: A succinct joke that characterizes both Leslie and April simultaneously. The fact that Leslie's first instinct is that this is an April prank is completely correct given April's history — which makes the reveal that it's real even better.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: London? Why would you want to explore London's history? It's all just a bunch of old stuff that happened before America was great.

jokes.text: Janet Napoli-freakin-tano? Oh, my God.
jokes.setup: Ann mentions Janet Napolitano won the same award.
jokes.punchline: Leslie inserts 'freakin'' into the middle of 'Napolitano' as an intensifier — her government-hero worship expressed as crude enthusiasm.
jokes.explanation: Infixing profanity into a proper noun ('Napoli-freakin-tano') is a great comedic technique — it's called expletive infixation. The choice of Janet Napolitano specifically, as a real government official Leslie would idolize, makes it perfectly character-specific. High quotability.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: My ideal honeymoon would involve a well-organized itinerary, productive activities, and efficient time management. We'd wake at 5 AM, complete a full day of purposeful tasks, enjoy a light dinner at 6 PM, and retire by 8:30 PM for optimal rest and recovery.

jokes.text: I can't believe we're at Hogwarts. / No, that's Buckingham Palace. Hogwarts is fictional. Do you know that? It's important to me that you know that.
jokes.setup: The gang arrives in London and sees Buckingham Palace.
jokes.punchline: Andy thinks they're at Hogwarts. Ben's correction escalates from factual ('that's Buckingham Palace') to genuinely concerned ('do you know that? It's important to me that you know that').
jokes.explanation: A beautiful Andy/Ben dynamic joke. Andy's confusion is perfect character. But Ben's escalation — from patient correction to 'it's important to me that you know that' — is the real joke, the barely-contained concern of a smart person who has accepted his lot in life. Ben's delivery is the engine.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Oh man, I just remembered this British kid called me Big Ben once. I thought it was so cool.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: BONG BONG BONG BONG

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Wait... do you think he was just calling me fat and British-sounding?

jokes.text: History began on July 4th, 1776. Everything before that was a mistake.
jokes.setup: Leslie announces she'll spend the day learning London's history.
jokes.punchline: Ron's talking-head: history began with American independence; everything before that was irrelevant — delivered as fact.
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best lines. The audacity of declaring all of pre-American history 'a mistake' while standing in London is magnificent. The two-sentence structure is perfect: first the absurd thesis, then the absolute dismissal. Extremely quotable, extremely character-specific — this line couldn't be delivered by anyone other than Ron Swanson. Comparable to the 8.0 anchor in quality.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Look, I'm just saying, if I'm going to do a British accent, I should probably know where Britain is. And I'm pretty sure it's somewhere near Australia, right?

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: They both have kangaroos and... British people. It's basically the same place.

jokes.text: Diane suggested we tag along to London for a honeymoon. I agreed because my love for her trumps my hatred for Europe.
jokes.setup: Ron explains why he's in London.
jokes.punchline: 'My love for her trumps my hatred for Europe' — a simple declarative sentence that reveals the hierarchy of Ron's values while also being deeply romantic in the most Ron-like way possible.
jokes.explanation: A near-perfect Ron Swanson joke. It's funny AND romantic in the most specifically Ron way imaginable. The construction is elegant: hatred of Europe is established as a baseline fact, and love for Diane is powerful enough to overcome it. The economy is extraordinary — 17 words that do the work of a scene. Very quotable.

dialogue.speaker: Lord Covington
dialogue.line: When addressing a British aristocrat, one must use the proper formal title. For instance, my full title is: His Most Serene and Exalted Lordship, the Earl of Covington, Duke of Hampshire, Marquess of Wessex, Count of Surrey, Baron of Kent, Knight of the Garter, Keeper of the Royal Seal, Protector of the Northern Reaches, and Custodian of the Ancient Chalice.

jokes.text: A steak dinner, a glass of Lagavulin whiskey, then vigorous lovemaking for two hours, and we're both asleep by 8:30.
jokes.setup: Ron describes his ideal honeymoon plan that was abandoned in favor of London.
jokes.punchline: Ron's honeymoon agenda is essentially: great food, great whiskey, efficient sex, early bedtime — the most utilitarian conception of romance possible, delivered with complete sincerity.
jokes.explanation: 'Vigorous lovemaking for two hours, and we're both asleep by 8:30' is a great gag — the specificity of 'two hours' and 'asleep by 8:30' strips romance down to its mechanical components and then schedules it. The Lagavulin name-drop is earned (it's Ron's established whiskey of choice). Great character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: Big Ben? More like Big Waste of Time. It's just a clock. I have a clock. It's called a sundial, and it's free, because the sun does the work.

jokes.text: Yeah, no. I want to quit and never come here again. / Okay, bye. / I can't believe I used to date you.
jokes.setup: Tom is dealing with the competitive threat to Rent A Swag. He calls April for support.
jokes.punchline: April's solution is to quit immediately and never return — delivered as helpful advice. Her 'okay, bye' when Tom hangs up is perfectly timed.
jokes.explanation: April's nihilistic advice ('just quit') is perfectly in character. Tom's exasperated 'I can't believe I used to date you' is a good tag that grounds it in their history.

dialogue.speaker: Ron Swanson
dialogue.line: I've seen the British landmarks. They're impressive, I'll give them that. But have you seen the architecture in Chicago? Now that's a city built by men who understand wood, steel, and the absence of government interference.

jokes.text: When life gives you lemons, you sell some of your grandma's jewelry and you go clubbing.
jokes.setup: Tom is despairing about losing business to the competitor. Jean-Ralphio offers advice.
jokes.punchline: Jean-Ralphio's version of 'when life gives you lemons' involves pawning grandma's jewelry and nightclubs — a complete non-sequitur that perfectly encapsulates his character.
jokes.explanation: A genuinely excellent joke. Taking the 'when life gives you lemons' template and replacing lemonade with 'sell grandma's jewelry and go clubbing' is both a perfect Jean-Ralphio character joke AND a funny subversion of a cliché. The specific detail of 'grandma's jewelry' elevates it from generic to vivid. High quotability. Comparable to the 8.0 anchor.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: What do you mean you don't accept American currency? American currency is the best currency. It has eagles on it.

jokes.text: So? I'm going to throw up. I ate too much cheese. I'll talk to you.
jokes.setup: Tom tells Jean-Ralphio his advice is not good.
jokes.punchline: Jean-Ralphio dismisses the conversation because he ate too much cheese and needs to vomit — delivered as a completely normal reason to end a business conversation.
jokes.explanation: The abruptness of 'I ate too much cheese' as a scene exit is perfectly in Jean-Ralphio's register. Funny in execution, good character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Ron Swanson
dialogue.line: The British royal family? A bunch of inbred aristocrats who sit around in castles all day pretending their bloodline matters. They don't produce anything, they don't build anything, they just exist and everyone bows to them. It's the most un-American thing I've ever heard of, and I hate it.

jokes.text: So, the only thing you did was stop drinking beer? / Yeah, I lost 50 pounds in one month. / How much beer were you drinking? / I know, right? / Probably too much.
jokes.setup: A man credits stopping beer drinking for massive weight loss.
jokes.punchline: The exchange implies the man was drinking an incomprehensible amount of beer — the understatement 'probably too much' is the button.
jokes.explanation: A functional background joke. The 50-pounds-in-one-month implication is funny and the exchange is tight. Not especially original or character-specific, but well-executed.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Alright, I'm here to confront my business rival. Let's do this.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Wait... what? You guys? What are you all doing here?

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Tom, we can explain.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: This is supposed to be my rival's office.

dialogue.speaker: Jerry
dialogue.line: Well, actually, we rented this space for the Parks Department event.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: So my business rival is... you people?

jokes.text: British people love me. There was this British kid in my high school who always called me Big Ben, and he would punch me really hard on the arm and go... Bong. Bong. Bong. / Oh, he might have hated me.
jokes.setup: Andy claims British people love him and offers this anecdote as evidence.
jokes.punchline: The story of 'Big Ben' — a classmate who punched him repeatedly while making clock sounds — Andy interpreted as affection but mid-story realizes was probably bullying. His self-correction 'oh, he might have hated me' is beautifully late.
jokes.explanation: This is one of the episode's best jokes. The structure is excellent: Andy builds his case ('British people love me'), provides evidence (the Big Ben story), and then — in real time — dismantles his own thesis ('oh, he might have hated me'). The Bong. Bong. Bong. sound effects mid-story are hilarious. The self-realization landing at 'might have hated me' — not 'definitely hated me,' just 'might have' — is perfect Andy Dwyer uncertainty. This is what great character comedy looks like.

dialogue.speaker: Dr. Saperstein
dialogue.line: Tom, I'm targeting you because you remind me of myself at your age - cocky, undisciplined, constantly making poor life choices.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: That's... oddly specific, Doc.

dialogue.speaker: Dr. Saperstein
dialogue.line: Yes, well, I've been in therapy for thirty years to deal with it. So now I project my failures onto my patients.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Should you be telling me this?

dialogue.speaker: Dr. Saperstein
dialogue.line: Probably not. That'll be an extra $200.

jokes.text: Real quick. Should I do a British accent? / Um... / I'm going to say no. / You sure? / Yeah. I can do one. / It's not very good, but I think I can pull it off.
jokes.setup: Andy and Ben are about to meet a British lord.
jokes.punchline: Andy's confidence that he can pull off an accent that is 'not very good' captures his complete lack of self-awareness — and Ben's brief hesitation before 'no' suggests he needed a moment to process the question.
jokes.explanation: Good character beat. The joke is Andy's total sincerity about a terrible plan. Ben's pause before answering suggests the question was so absurd it required processing.

dialogue.speaker: Dr. Saperstein
dialogue.line: Her BMW was destroyed, and we had to move her to public school.

dialogue.speaker: Dr. Saperstein
dialogue.line: The contrast between that car and her education is going to haunt me forever.

jokes.text: Ugh, great. All right, well. I guess we'll take the meeting anyway. After all, we did come all the way down under. / No.
jokes.setup: Ben explains they're in England, not Australia.
jokes.punchline: Andy thinks England is 'down under' — confusing England with Australia. Ben's single 'No.' is maximally economical.
jokes.explanation: Ben's single-word 'No.' is doing a lot of work — it's dismissal, correction, and exhaustion in one syllable. Andy's geographic confusion is well within character. The economy of Ben's response is excellent.

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: Do you hear that? That's my heartbeat.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: That's beautiful.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Whoa, whoa, whoa. Ann, is that a file folder in your shirt?

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: What? No!

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Your heart is beating in triplicate.

jokes.text: No, no, no, I'm kidding. I'm kidding. Please call me Eddie. / Oh. Thank God. / I knew that other name must have been a stupid joke. / Andy. / No, no, no. No, he's absolutely right. It's an absurd name.
jokes.setup: Lord Covington delivers an absurdly long formal title, then reveals he's joking — call him Eddie.
jokes.punchline: Ben is relieved. Andy blunders by agreeing the name was 'stupid.' Ben tries to correct him. Lord Covington agrees with Andy — 'it's an absurd name.'
jokes.explanation: A well-constructed three-beat exchange. Andy's social blunder ('must have been a stupid joke') is cringe-inducing in the best way, and Lord Covington's gracious agreement defuses it while being funnier than a correction would have been.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: I'm claiming the blue helicopter.

dialogue.speaker: Lord Covington
dialogue.line: But sir, there are rules posted here quite clearly.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: I don't care about rules, I want that helicopter.

dialogue.speaker: Lord Covington
dialogue.line: Well then, I'm afraid I must insist. The playground regulations are quite explicit. Children under 12 only.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: I'm an adult, so what?

dialogue.speaker: Lord Covington
dialogue.line: Then you cannot use the blue helicopter. A gentleman always respects the rules, even over social hierarchy.

jokes.text: Look. A clock. We don't have that in America.
jokes.setup: Leslie is asking Ron to choose a London bus tour. Ron has been obstinately unimpressed by everything.
jokes.punchline: Ron points at Big Ben and declares it 'a clock' they don't have in America — both dismissing one of the world's most famous landmarks and willfully ignoring the London sightseeing context.
jokes.explanation: Reducing Big Ben to 'a clock' is a perfect Ron Swanson anti-European tourist joke. The deadpan delivery implied by 'we don't have that in America' — as though America lacks clocks — adds a layer of oblivious absurdism. Very quotable and highly character-specific.

dialogue.speaker: Lord Covington
dialogue.line: My family owns vast estates across the countryside, multiple townhouses in London, and several country clubs.

dialogue.speaker: Lord Covington
dialogue.line: Actually, I forgot to mention we also own half of Scotland and a controlling interest in the Bank of England.

jokes.text: You call that a tower? Try the Sears Tower, friend.
jokes.setup: Ron continues his tourist monologue while dismissing London landmarks.
jokes.punchline: Ron compares a London tower (likely the Tower of London) to the Sears Tower, Chicago — proudly American, completely missing the point of being a tourist.
jokes.explanation: Solid continuation of Ron's xenophobic tourist bit. Less original than the clock joke — comparing American architecture favorably to British is a well-worn bit — but saved by Ron's total sincerity.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Do you have ice cream in England?

dialogue.speaker: Lord Covington
dialogue.line: Do we have ice cream? Of course we have ice cream. We invented civilization.

jokes.text: Of course you do. That's the most wonderful piece of paper in the world. Accept it. / Very sorry, sir. / Fine. Enjoy the fact that your royal overlords are a frail old woman and a tiny baby.
jokes.setup: Ron tries to pay with American currency at a London gift shop and is refused.
jokes.punchline: Ron's parting shot about the British monarchy — 'a frail old woman and a tiny baby' — as their 'royal overlords' is a characteristically blunt Ron Swanson dismissal.
jokes.explanation: The dismissal of the Queen as 'a frail old woman' and the heir as 'a tiny baby' (presumably Prince George, recently born) is pleasingly blunt Ron Swanson anti-monarchism. The escalation from 'most wonderful piece of paper in the world' to the royal insult is well-structured.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: April, I really need your honest feedback on this speech. What do you think?

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: It's too long. Also, add more jokes about death. And replace all the words with the word 'butt.' Actually, just make the whole thing a interpretive dance. In the dark. With no music. Just screaming.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: That's... not helpful.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: You asked for honesty.

jokes.text: Ann and Chris? What are they doing here? [Tom discovers his rival is at Ann's OB/GYN]
jokes.setup: Tom has been tracking down his mysterious competitor to an address — dramatically bursting into the office.
jokes.punchline: The address is Ann's OB/GYN office, where Ann and Chris are getting a sonogram. Tom's dramatic entrance is completely deflated by the mundane context.
jokes.explanation: A great structural gag — the noir investigation trope (tracking the villain to his lair, dramatic entrance) deflated by 'it's an OB/GYN office.' The subverted expectation is well-built. Rewatch bonus for the setup.

dialogue.speaker: Kathryn Pinewood
dialogue.line: You went to Europe. That makes you European.

jokes.text: You destroyed my family. First, you screwed my son out of your business. And then, you stole my daughter's virginity.
jokes.setup: Dr. Saperstein explains why he's trying to destroy Tom's business.
jokes.punchline: The escalation from 'screwed my son out of business' to 'stole my daughter's virginity' is a dramatic and funny tonal escalation — the second accusation is so much more personal and extreme.
jokes.explanation: The escalation from business grievance to the personal/sexual accusation is well-timed. Saperstein's absolute seriousness makes it funnier. The absurdity of 'stole my daughter's virginity' as a business crime is a good comedic juxtaposition.

dialogue.speaker: Perd
dialogue.line: I have a question. If you were to hypothetically have an affair with someone, would that someone be a man? Would that someone be a woman? Or would that someone be, say, a man, but you're a woman, but in a different way?

dialogue.speaker: Perd
dialogue.line: You know what, I'm not even sure what I'm asking anymore.

jokes.text: Then, you smashed up her BMW. I had to buy her a new one so she could drive to divinity school.
jokes.setup: Dr. Saperstein continues listing Tom's crimes against his family.
jokes.punchline: The detail 'so she could drive to divinity school' — the daughter going to divinity school after all this — is a wonderfully absurd detail that adds texture to the Saperstein family dysfunction.
jokes.explanation: The 'divinity school' detail is funny in its specificity — it adds a dimension to the Saperstein family while being completely unexpected. Good escalation.

dialogue.speaker: Jean-Ralphio
dialogue.line: I told Tom I was a professional snowboarder. Then I said I won the X-Games twice. Then I said I invented a new snowboarding move called the Jean-Ralphio 720 Spin Kick. Then I said that move is now in the Winter Olympics. Then I said I'm the all-time medal leader in Winter Olympics history. Then I said the Winter Olympics renamed themselves the Jean-Ralphio Games. Then I said I'm actually the Winter Olympics.

jokes.text: And there it is, the heartbeat. Everything sounds perfect. / Oh. This is the moment we were dreaming of. You and me and our baby. And Tom and his weird feud with our doctor.
jokes.setup: A serious/emotional moment — hearing the baby's heartbeat for the first time — interrupted by the ongoing Tom/Saperstein argument in the same room.
jokes.punchline: Ann's affectionate summation includes 'and Tom and his weird feud with our doctor' as part of their perfect moment — she's rolled with the absurdity completely.
jokes.explanation: A beautifully constructed tonal whiplash. The emotional climax (baby heartbeat) is undercut by Ann casually folding Tom's feud into her tender moment. Her acceptance of the absurd chaos as part of life is a great character beat. The line itself is very quotable for its construction.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: They filled it with vegetables instead of candy. As if beating a piñata of my face wasn't humiliating enough, they had to make it educational.

jokes.text: Would you like to play with them? / Oh, would I? I call the blue one. I call... Aw. / Okay, you get the blue one. / Andy, we are guests of Lord Covington. Maybe you should let him... / Play with the blue helicopter. / What are you talking about, dude? I called it. / He called it. That's the rule.
jokes.setup: Lord Covington reveals remote control helicopters during a formal charity pitch meeting.
jokes.punchline: Andy immediately abandons all professional pretense to fight over the blue helicopter — insisting the 'I called it' rule applies to business meetings with English lords. Lord Covington, magnificently, agrees: 'He called it. That's the rule.'
jokes.explanation: A great joke built on Andy's complete inability to behave professionally, elevated by Lord Covington's unexpected validation. 'He called it. That's the rule.' — the lord's solemn agreement with children's playground logic — is funnier than any correction would have been. Shows why Lord Covington and Andy are kindred spirits.

dialogue.speaker: Lord Covington
dialogue.line: I found a Fabergé egg, three Louis XVI chairs, and my great-uncle Reginald. Turns out he'd been missing since 1987.

jokes.text: Dude, awesome. I think I broke mine. / Oh, bummer.
jokes.setup: Andy and Lord Covington are playing with the helicopters instead of discussing the charity.
jokes.punchline: Lord Covington's 'oh, bummer' — delivered as a proper English gentleman — is funny for applying British understatement to a destroyed toy.
jokes.explanation: A minor but functional joke. Lord Covington saying 'oh, bummer' is a small cultural collision — the British lord adopting American slang. Light and charming.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: So you're offering me the job?

dialogue.speaker: Eddie
dialogue.line: What? No. I'm offering it to Andy.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: But... I have an MBA, I've worked in government, I have a proven track record of—

dialogue.speaker: Eddie
dialogue.line: Yeah, yeah. But Andy's more fun at parties.

jokes.text: What else does your family own? / Well, um, have you heard of Scotland?
jokes.setup: Lord Covington is listing family properties while the charity pitch has been abandoned.
jokes.punchline: 'Have you heard of Scotland?' — delivered as if Scotland might be a niche property most people wouldn't know about — implies the family owns an entire country.
jokes.explanation: Five words that are perfectly constructed. The casual inquiry 'have you heard of Scotland?' — as if Scotland is an obscure property they might own — is a brilliant understatement joke. The implication that a person might NOT have heard of Scotland makes it funnier. Exceptional economy. One of the episode's best lines.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: I assume you want me to stay and help you with all this.

dialogue.speaker: Lord Covington
dialogue.line: Actually, I'd prefer if Andy stayed. His childlike enthusiasm is far more refreshing than your constant need to optimize and organize everything.

jokes.text: Oh, you know what I want? Ice cream. Do you guys have that here? Ice cream? It's so good. You have to get it. It's like scoops and it comes on a cone. Do you have that here? / We have it. Of course we have it. Where do you think you are, the moon?
jokes.setup: Andy interrupts the charity discussion to ask about ice cream.
jokes.punchline: Andy explains ice cream to a British lord as if he might not know what it is. Lord Covington's 'where do you think you are, the moon?' is a perfect exasperated response.
jokes.explanation: Andy explaining ice cream to an English lord ('it's like scoops and it comes on a cone') is fantastic. The innocence of Andy's explanation and Lord Covington's incredulous 'the moon?' response builds a great comedic rapport. The specific description 'scoops and it comes on a cone' is perfect Andy-level description.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: That reindeer was amazing at the party!

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I know, right? So graceful, so magical...

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: We ate him.

jokes.text: That would be awesome if we were. / Yeah.
jokes.setup: Lord Covington sarcastically asks if Andy thinks they're on the moon.
jokes.punchline: Andy takes this completely literally and enthuses about how awesome it would be to be on the moon. Lord Covington simply agrees.
jokes.explanation: Andy's literal interpretation of a rhetorical question is perfect character comedy. But the real joke is Lord Covington's 'yeah' — he genuinely agrees. This brief moment reveals why they're kindred spirits and why Covington will eventually ask Andy to stay. The economy is extraordinary.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: You know what? Pawnee is a terrible town with terrible people and I'm done pretending otherwise.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: And the worst part is... you're all a bunch of idiots.

jokes.text: What do I do with this? / Just throw it there. Roger will pick it up. / Oh.
jokes.setup: Ben is holding some item and asks what to do with it.
jokes.punchline: Lord Covington casually notes 'Roger will pick it up' — implying a servant named Roger exists for exactly this purpose. Ben's simple 'Oh' registers the enormous class difference.
jokes.explanation: A gentle class-difference joke. Ben's 'oh' does a lot of work — it's the quiet acknowledgment of a world entirely foreign to him. The specificity of the servant's name (Roger) is a nice touch.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: And that is why Pawnee, Indiana is the greatest town in the world. We have the most beautiful parks, the most hardworking citizens, and the most... poopy... heads in any neighboring town.

jokes.text: I think you should lose the first line and the last line, and all of the other lines, and instead, just walk up to the mic and meow really loudly for eight minutes.
jokes.setup: Leslie asks Ben what he thinks of her award speech.
jokes.punchline: Ben's critique escalates from 'lose the first line' to 'lose the last line' to 'all the other lines' — then instead of helpful revision suggests she meow for eight minutes.
jokes.explanation: A beautifully constructed escalation joke. The structure — lose the first line, lose the last line, lose ALL the other lines — builds perfectly before exploding into the absurdist 'meow really loudly for eight minutes.' The specificity of 'eight minutes' is key. This is excellent writing: the escalation setup is tight, the pivot to meowing is unexpected, and the specific duration makes it funnier. Very quotable.

dialogue.speaker: Donna
dialogue.line: I know things about all of you. I know Tom's favorite position is spooning, but only if he's the big spoon. I know he cries after.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Okay, why would you say that out loud?

jokes.text: She's gallivanting around Europe, like some kind of European.
jokes.setup: Leslie's political opponent is attacking her for being in London.
jokes.punchline: 'Gallivanting around Europe like some kind of European' — the circular insult of accusing someone in Europe of being European as if it's damning.
jokes.explanation: A great piece of political satire. The tautological accusation ('like some kind of European') encapsulates a certain strain of parochial American politics perfectly. The redundancy is the joke — being European while in Europe is the worst thing Pinewood can say. Very quotable and immediately applicable to real-world political rhetoric.

dialogue.speaker: Jerry
dialogue.line: They're like little animals, rooting around for milk. It's actually kind of disturbing when you think about it.

jokes.text: How did they get that picture? Facebook. / But I just put... / Facebook. / Isn't it a... / Mmm. Facebook.
jokes.setup: Leslie is shocked her opponents found a photo of her in London.
jokes.punchline: Every time Leslie begins to question how, Ben or Ann simply says 'Facebook' — three times — as Leslie keeps trying to construct a defense.
jokes.explanation: The triple 'Facebook' — cutting off each of Leslie's attempts at a defense — is a perfectly executed running gag within a single exchange. The structure is tight: Leslie attempts three times to rationalize, gets cut off each time with the same single word. The word 'mmm' before the third 'Facebook' adds a chef's-kiss quality.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: I went to Piccadilly Circus expecting an actual circus with acrobats and clowns. Instead it's just a traffic circle with a statue of Eros. I was so disappointed.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: But then I marveled at how let down I was.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: You marveled at it?

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Yeah, I marveled at it. Why, is that weird?

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: No, it's just... you can't marvel at something being disappointing.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Why not? I marvel at lots of things. I marveled at a sandwich the other day.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: Okay, you need to stop using that word.

jokes.text: Well, we conducted a Perd Poll and asked this question. Do you think Leslie Knope should be in England? Do you not think that, or do you not think that? / 35% said they were confused by the way the question was posed.
jokes.setup: Perd Hapley conducts a poll about Leslie.
jokes.punchline: Perd's poll gives only negative options ('do you not think that, or do you not think that?'), with zero affirmative choice — and 35% were confused by the question itself.
jokes.explanation: A masterpiece of Perd Hapley character comedy. His poll literally has no option for 'yes, she should be in England' — a perfect parody of biased push-polling. The 35% confusion figure is a brilliant touch: it validates the confusingness of the question while being presented as a normal poll result. Perd's journalistic incompetence has never been rendered with more precision. Very high character integration — this joke is impossible without Perd.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: You once spent $300 on a shoe that was just a shoe. Not a special shoe. Just a regular shoe.

jokes.text: Well, not to Indiana. But there's a 9:00 redeye to Lisbon. And then, I can catch the 4:30 AM back to Edinburgh, connect through Houston, head on up to Cincinnati and then, rent a car, drive around 90, and I'll be home two hours earlier than if I flew home as planned. Easy breezy.
jokes.setup: Leslie wants to fly home immediately in response to the political controversy.
jokes.punchline: Leslie has already worked out a comically convoluted route home — Lisbon → Edinburgh → Houston → Cincinnati → drive on I-90 — that arrives two hours earlier, described as 'easy breezy.'
jokes.explanation: The absurdity of the routing escalates beautifully — Lisbon to Edinburgh to Houston to Cincinnati to a rental car — and the punchline of 'easy breezy' after all that is perfect. It also reveals Leslie's brain: she has already done this math and found an answer. The detail of 'drive around 90' (I-90) grounds it in specific Midwestern geography.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I'm fine, I'm fine. I just took some Ambien and I'm a little jet-lagged, so I might be hallucinating slightly, but I'm good.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Wait, why is Ben made of corn?

jokes.text: That is so weird. That is so... Oh, you know what? Honestly, now that I'm thinking about it, this may be it. I actually told him that Rent A Swag was my idea, and that you had stole it from me. / Why would you say that?
jokes.setup: Jean-Ralphio is performing outrage at the idea that his father believed Tom screwed him over.
jokes.punchline: Mid-protest, Jean-Ralphio remembers that he himself told his father this lie — the 'I can't believe it' performance collapses into confession.
jokes.explanation: Jean-Ralphio working himself up into righteous indignation and then self-deflating when he remembers he's the actual culprit is perfect Jean-Ralphio. The beat of 'that is so... oh, you know what' is beautifully written — you can hear the gears turning.

dialogue.speaker: Jean-Ralphio
dialogue.line: I didn't lie to my father. I told him I was gonna be something great, and I am great. I'm doing great things. I'm a business man, I'm an entrepreneur, I'm very smart.

jokes.text: I also have something to say. I also told him that you made me sign up for a bunch of credit cards, and then maxed them out by buying illegal white jaguar fur coats. / That's probably not relevant. / It's probably not relevant, though. / I guess. No, definitely.
jokes.setup: Jean-Ralphio has just confessed the initial lie. He adds more.
jokes.punchline: The 'illegal white jaguar fur coats' is a perfectly specific absurd detail. The shared back-and-forth about relevance — where both agree it's 'probably not relevant' while clearly it very much is — is great.
jokes.explanation: The specificity of 'illegal white jaguar fur coats' is inspired — it's so specific and so extreme that it's clearly a fabrication born from creative desperation. The mutual 'probably not relevant' agreement — which is patently false — is a great shared-logic comedy beat between two characters with terrible judgment.

dialogue.speaker: Jean-Ralphio
dialogue.line: Yo, yo, yo! Why you gotta be all serious like that? Life's too short to not have fun, bro!

dialogue.speaker: Jean-Ralphio
dialogue.line: You're like a... a sad little potato!

jokes.text: Not it! / Ooh, you got me! / Uh-oh. Uh-oh. Uh-oh. Uh-oh. Uh-oh.
jokes.setup: Tom says one of them has to tell Dr. Saperstein the truth.
jokes.punchline: Jean-Ralphio immediately calls 'not it!' and Tom is stuck. Jean-Ralphio's cascade of 'uh-oh' taunts at Tom's predicament.
jokes.explanation: The 'not it!' playground logic applied to a serious adult problem is good character comedy. The cascade of 'uh-oh' from Jean-Ralphio is the right comedic texture for his character. Functional and enjoyable.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: That's a lump sum.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: What?

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: A lump sum. It's a cartoon character. He fights crime at night.

jokes.text: Okay, fine. You know what? I'm going to do the unthinkable. I'm going to have a short, honest conversation with my father.
jokes.setup: Jean-Ralphio is stuck having to deal with his father.
jokes.punchline: An honest conversation with his own father is described as 'the unthinkable' — positioning basic human communication as an extreme sacrifice.
jokes.explanation: Jean-Ralphio framing basic family honesty as 'the unthinkable' perfectly characterizes his relationship to truthfulness. The escalating framing — 'okay, fine,' 'you know what,' 'I'm going to do the unthinkable' — before a completely normal sentence is well-structured.

dialogue.speaker: Chris
dialogue.line: I prefer names based on how healthy they sound. Like, 'Sebastian' sounds very healthy. 'Broccoli' sounds healthy too, but I don't think we can name our kid that.

jokes.text: Once, on my birthday, the town trained a reindeer to do a dance for me. / It was beautiful / and the reindeer was delicious.
jokes.setup: Ulee is describing how much her hometown of Silkeborg loves her.
jokes.punchline: After describing the reindeer's beautiful dance, she adds '...and the reindeer was delicious' — implying they ate it immediately after.
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best jokes. The structure is perfect: a heartwarming story about a dancing reindeer on her birthday pivots without warning to the reindeer being eaten. The deadpan conjunction 'and the reindeer was delicious' — as if this is a natural continuation of the warmth — is brilliant dark comedy. High originality, perfect economy, exceptional structure. Comparable to or exceeding the 8.0 anchor.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: Dear Leslie, You are the most wonderful person I know. You have changed my life in ways I never thought possible. You are my best friend and I love you. With all my heart, April Ludgate. P.S. Just kidding, you suck.

jokes.text: Aluminium. / Okay. / You say it. You say it. You say it. / It's allumilum. / Allumilum?
jokes.setup: Leslie and Ulee discover the pronunciation difference between American 'aluminum' and British/European 'aluminium.'
jokes.punchline: Leslie's version 'allumilum' is a complete mispronunciation of both versions — worse than either original.
jokes.explanation: A functional word-play/pronunciation joke. Leslie creating a third, worse word ('allumilum') by attempting both versions is funny. Good character integration — Leslie would enthusiastically try and fail.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: I don't understand why we're standing by this lake reading poetry. Poetry is a waste of paper. And Scotland is a waste of geography.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: The only romantic thing I need is a good scotch and a woman who doesn't ask me how I'm feeling. This poem is fourteen lines too long.

jokes.text: I honestly don't know whether they're good or bad. / If I may. / Ours is great. / Brilliant. I'm in.
jokes.setup: Lord Covington admits he doesn't know how to evaluate charity pitches despite hearing hundreds. Ben offers a solution.
jokes.punchline: Ben's entire pitch is 'ours is great.' Lord Covington immediately agrees: 'Brilliant. I'm in.' The most successful charity pitch in history takes four words.
jokes.explanation: A beautifully constructed anti-climax. The entire charity meeting — disrupted by helicopters, ice cream, and geography lessons — resolves in four words. Ben's confident one-line pitch works because Lord Covington literally just admitted he can't tell good from bad. The structure is outstanding: the elaborate setup, the simple solution. Very quotable.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Oh my god, you look so hot in that wig. We should roleplay. You're a British barrister and I'm an American woman who needs legal advice.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Actually, no. Forget I said that. That's weird.

jokes.text: Is that a goose that just flew by the window? / Oh, it's a plastic bag. Did you see that?
jokes.setup: Lord Covington has just offered Andy the London position — a major life moment.
jokes.punchline: Andy completely derails the moment because he thinks he saw a goose, which turns out to be a plastic bag — and is equally excited about the plastic bag.
jokes.explanation: Perfectly character-specific. Andy's equal enthusiasm for the possible goose and the plastic bag — during his biggest professional opportunity — is the Andy Dwyer character perfectly rendered. The beat of 'oh, it's a plastic bag. Did you see that?' with undiminished excitement is beautiful.

jokes.text: I meant Andy. I want Andy to stay.
jokes.setup: Ben assumes Lord Covington wants HIM to stay in London when he offers the position.
jokes.punchline: Covington wanted Andy — the man who ate ice cream, broke a helicopter, thought they were on the moon, and is currently distracted by a plastic bag.
jokes.explanation: A perfect structural reversal. The entire meeting has been Ben trying to make the pitch while Andy derails it — and the punchline is that Andy's chaos is exactly what Covington wanted. The callback to everything Andy did in the meeting makes this a satisfying payoff for an extended comedic setup. The economy of 'I meant Andy' is perfect.

jokes.text: Well, Pawnee, Indiana, is a wonderful town, and I love it. But they hate me, and they're trying to kick me out of office. One time, they made a piñata of my face. And then, everybody in the town came and took turns hitting it with a stick. And they filled it with broccoli just to add insult to injury.
jokes.setup: Ulee has been talking about being beloved by Silkeborg. Leslie is asked about her hometown.
jokes.punchline: The escalating specifics of Leslie's humiliation — piñata, whole town hitting it, filled with broccoli 'to add insult to injury' — is the inverse of Ulee's adulation.
jokes.explanation: The broccoli detail is inspired — filling a piñata with broccoli instead of candy to maximize the insult is both a funny specific escalation and a perfect encapsulation of Pawnee's relationship with Leslie. 'To add insult to injury' delivered as genuine explanation rather than idiom is a great touch. Very quotable.

jokes.text: Pawnee is filled with a bunch of peepee-heads.
jokes.setup: Leslie has been increasingly worked up about Pawnee's ingratitude during her award acceptance speech.
jokes.punchline: The escalation of frustration — from professional critique to 'peepee-heads' — crashes from civic eloquence to kindergarten-level insult.
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best lines. 'Peepee-heads' is the perfect release valve for a speech that has been building toward Leslie's unfiltered frustration. The infantile insult deployed at an international awards ceremony is a tonal collision that works perfectly. Extremely quotable. The follow-up 'I'm sorry I said peepee-heads' makes it even better — the immediate regret suggesting she knows exactly how wrong that was.

jokes.text: I'm sorry I said peepee-heads.
jokes.setup: Leslie just called all of Pawnee 'peepee-heads' in an international award speech.
jokes.punchline: The immediate apology — which apologizes specifically for the word choice rather than the sentiment — is Leslie Knope in full: she knows exactly which part was wrong.
jokes.explanation: The perfect button to the peepee-heads joke. Leslie apologizes only for the word — not for calling them peepee-heads per se, just for saying it out loud. This tiny coda perfectly encapsulates Leslie: self-aware about her public presentation, completely unrepentant about her feelings. Very quotable on its own.

jokes.text: That's my boss.
jokes.setup: Leslie has just given the 'peepee-heads' speech to an international audience.
jokes.punchline: Ben's talking-head deadpan: 'That's my boss.' Three words that carry enormous pride, embarrassment, and resignation simultaneously.
jokes.explanation: Economy at its absolute peak — three words that do the work of a paragraph. The camera cut to Ben saying 'that's my boss' after the peepee-heads speech is a perfect mockumentary beat. It works because the three words could mean completely different things: embarrassment, pride, or both simultaneously. The best possible response to the situation.

jokes.text: Even if that air is filled with the foul stench of European socialism.
jokes.setup: Ron tells Leslie to get fresh air — then qualifies it.
jokes.punchline: Ron's suggestion of fresh air is immediately undercut by 'the foul stench of European socialism' — he can't give helpful advice without his politics infecting it.
jokes.explanation: Ron's libertarian/anti-European politics slipping into even basic practical advice is perfectly in character. 'The foul stench of European socialism' as a description of London air is inspired and very Ron-specific.

jokes.text: When did you make the switch to boxer briefs? / Yesterday. / Okay, please stop looking at him.
jokes.setup: Donna has just impressed everyone with her observational skills on Ann.
jokes.punchline: Donna turns the same forensic gaze on Chris's underwear, which is both an escalation of her power and immediately creepy — Ann has to intervene.
jokes.explanation: A perfect escalation of the preceding joke. Donna's detective skills extend to Chris's underwear, which Chris matter-of-factly confirms. Ann's 'please stop looking at him' is the ideal button. Well-constructed and earns laughs from both the absurdity and Ann's reaction.

jokes.text: Well, April does that all the time. She nominated Ann for Motocross Driver of the Year Award, just so she could get a rejection letter.
jokes.setup: Ron is pointing out that April nominated Leslie for this award as evidence that April respects her.
jokes.punchline: Leslie counters that April regularly nominates people for awards they can't possibly win — specifically to get the rejection letter — as a prank.
jokes.explanation: April nominating Ann for 'Motocross Driver of the Year' specifically to generate a rejection letter is a perfect April Ludgate joke — it reveals the depth of her devotion to petty cruelty, the specificity of the execution (actually wanting the rejection letter), and the absurdity of the award category. This is great character writing — a side character's personality perfectly rendered in one sentence.

jokes.text: Before my kids, I looked a lot like you, Chris. / I am very sad. Please stop talking.
jokes.setup: Jerry is enthusiastically discussing pregnancy with Chris.
jokes.punchline: Jerry's implication that having children ruined his physique — comparing himself to the famously fit Chris — devastates Chris, whose response is a perfect two-sentence breakdown.
jokes.explanation: A great two-character joke. Jerry as a preview of Chris's post-children future is both funny and devastating. 'I am very sad. Please stop talking.' is Chris at his most human — the optimism completely obliterated in two sentences. The economy of Chris's response is excellent.

jokes.text: This is London, Ron. There's a pub over there, there's a pub over there, there's a pub between those two butcher shops.
jokes.setup: Ron says he'd offer to buy Leslie a drink but doesn't know where that would happen.
jokes.punchline: Leslie's pub inventory — including the hyper-specific 'pub between those two butcher shops' — reveals she has been clocking London's pubs despite claiming to not enjoy travel.
jokes.explanation: The specificity of 'the pub between those two butcher shops' is a good detail. The punchline is Ron's response — immediately wanting to stop at the butcher shops first — which is very Ron.

jokes.text: Because they are rooting around for that nipple. / Give it to me. I want milk.
jokes.setup: Jerry is explaining newborn behavior to Chris and Ann in a medical waiting context.
jokes.punchline: Jerry, apparently lost in his own memories, suddenly delivers a baby's-voice impression: 'Give it to me. I want milk.' — completely collapsing the boundary between explanation and re-enactment.
jokes.explanation: Jerry going method on his newborn explanation — providing a voice for the baby — is creepy and funny in exactly the right proportion. The line 'Give it to me. I want milk.' in a baby-like tone from a middle-aged government employee is genuinely jarring comedy.

jokes.text: Like how they drive on the other side of the road? / Do they? / I'll be damned.
jokes.setup: Andy is listing reasons why England is too different for him to stay.
jokes.punchline: Andy lists British left-hand driving as one of the differences. When April confirms it, he responds 'I'll be damned' — as if this is a brand new revelation he has never heard.
jokes.explanation: Andy's 'I'll be damned' at learning about British driving — delivered as genuine amazement at something universally known — is a solid Andy Dwyer ignorance joke. The delivery implied by the script ('do they?') is perfect.

jokes.text: Or, like, the Piccadilly Circus we went to? Not even a circus. There's no elephants. There is no cotton candies. No clowns. One bearded lady. She got all rude when I marveled at her.
jokes.setup: Andy is listing the differences between England and America.
jokes.punchline: Andy was genuinely expecting a circus at Piccadilly Circus, found only one qualifying element (a bearded lady), approached her as a circus act, and was rebuffed.
jokes.explanation: Excellent Andy joke. The escalating list of circus elements he expected ('no elephants, no cotton candies, no clowns') followed by the discovery of 'one bearded lady' who 'got all rude when I marveled at her' is perfectly constructed. The word 'marveled' is doing a lot of work — Andy genuinely marveling at a random woman as if she were a circus attraction.

jokes.text: The Piccadilly Circus we went to? Not even a circus. There's no elephants. There is no cotton candies. / No clowns. / One bearded lady. She got all rude when I marveled at her.
jokes.setup: Andy is listing England's strange differences.
jokes.punchline: Andy went to Piccadilly Circus expecting an actual circus. The escalation from 'no elephants, no cotton candy, no clowns' to 'one bearded lady — she got all rude when I marveled at her' is perfect.
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's finest jokes. Andy mistaking Piccadilly Circus for a circus is a wonderful premise. But the escalation — cataloguing circus elements that were absent — building to 'one bearded lady who got all rude when I marveled at her' is a perfect comedic structure. The specificity that Andy 'marveled' at her (presumably a random hairy woman) and that she was 'rude' about it — as if Andy's marveling was the reasonable response — is exceptional character comedy. This is what distinguishes Parks and Rec: Andy's version of this is better than any version of this joke could be with a different character.

jokes.text: Remote control helicopters, talks funny. Total package.
jokes.setup: April asks if Andy likes Lord Covington.
jokes.punchline: Andy's summary of 'total package' for Lord Covington: remote control helicopters and a funny accent. These are his complete evaluation criteria for a patron.
jokes.explanation: A perfect Andy joke. His complete evaluation criteria for a potential employer: toys and a funny voice. 'Total package' applied to these criteria is a perfect deadpan. The economy is outstanding.

jokes.text: You shined shoes for over two years and never made a profit. / Come on. You can hack this.
jokes.setup: Andy says he doesn't know how to run a non-profit.
jokes.punchline: April reframes his shoe-shining failure as relevant non-profit experience — 'you never made a profit' — it's technically true.
jokes.explanation: A brilliant wordplay/logic joke. April's reframing of Andy's failed shoe business as non-profit experience is technically correct while being completely absurd. The deadpan 'you can hack this' follow-up — as if this is genuine encouragement — makes it land perfectly. This is the best kind of wordplay: it also characterizes both speakers perfectly. One of the episode's top-tier jokes.

jokes.text: But to replace you, I am going to have to build a scarecrow replica of you and take it to the movies. Seems like the only logical solution.
jokes.setup: April is accepting that Andy will stay in London.
jokes.punchline: April's plan to cope with Andy's absence: build a scarecrow version of him and take it to the movies — presented with complete logical conviction ('seems like the only logical solution').
jokes.explanation: April's plan to build a scarecrow of Andy and take it to the movies is both a deeply strange expression of love and a perfectly April Ludgate solution. The tag 'seems like the only logical solution' — delivered with complete conviction — is excellent. This joke reveals April's feelings through the most April-possible coping mechanism. High originality, strong character integration, very quotable.

jokes.text: Tom. Lawyer guy. Daddy.
jokes.setup: Jean-Ralphio is about to confess the truth to his father in a room with Tom and their lawyer.
jokes.punchline: Jean-Ralphio addresses everyone in the room as 'Tom. Lawyer guy. Daddy.' — the final greeting reducing his father to the last slot in a list, yet the most emotionally loaded.
jokes.explanation: The descending register from 'Tom' (name) to 'Lawyer guy' (job title) to 'Daddy' (intimate term) — with 'Daddy' the most emotionally loaded but delivered in the same flat register — is a great structural choice. Jean-Ralphio has equal emotional distance from everyone in the room, which tells us everything.

jokes.text: Daddy. Daddy. Come on. I lie to you all the time. All those math camps I said I went to? I don't even know what a math camp is. / So, all those postcards that you sent me, all those trophies that you'd won... / Trophies I bought.
jokes.setup: Jean-Ralphio is trying to explain that lying to his father is normal, not exceptional.
jokes.punchline: Dr. Saperstein discovers that trophies from math camp — which he presumably displayed with pride — were purchased fakes. 'Trophies I bought' is the devastating two-word confirmation.
jokes.explanation: A beautifully structured escalation. Jean-Ralphio using 'I lie to you all the time' as reassurance builds to the reveal that his math camp success story was entirely fabricated — complete with purchased trophies. The structure (Saperstein's dawning horror cut off by 'Trophies I bought') is excellent. The joke reveals an entire history of deception in a single moment.

jokes.text: I have done nothing wrong. Ever, in my life. I know this.
jokes.setup: Mona-Lisa interjects during the family confession scene.
