jokes.punchline: Mona-Lisa's declaration — 'I have done nothing wrong. Ever, in my life. I know this.' — delivered with absolute certainty, is both obviously false and deeply character-specific.
jokes.explanation: Three sentences of total narcissistic certainty. 'I know this' is the key — it's not a plea or a defense, it's a statement of fact from someone with complete conviction in her own righteousness. Very quotable, and one of the better lines in the Saperstein subplot. Could only be said by this character.

jokes.text: Tell me you love us, and then, admit this guy looks like Beaker from the Muppets.
jokes.setup: Mona-Lisa is trying to get her father to reconcile.
jokes.punchline: She ties the family reconciliation to Saperstein admitting that Tom looks like Beaker from the Muppets — an irrelevant condition that reveals her priorities.
jokes.explanation: Tying familial reconciliation to the Beaker comparison is a perfect Mona-Lisa move — she needs to win a petty point even during a heartfelt moment. The Beaker reference itself is funny; Tom Haverford does have some Beaker energy.

jokes.text: These two have been huge disappointments to me. / Come on. You love us. / Tell me you love us, and then, admit this guy looks like Beaker from the Muppets. / Dad. / But seriously, what are we doing here? / What are we doing here, Dad? / Why are we here?
jokes.setup: Saperstein has declared his children huge disappointments.
jokes.punchline: Jean-Ralphio and Mona-Lisa's strategy to get their father's love: ignore the accusation, demand affirmation, derail into the Beaker comparison, then collectively chant existential questions at him.
jokes.explanation: The trio's collective dysfunction is well-portrayed. Jean-Ralphio and Mona-Lisa have zero ability to respond to direct criticism, instead pivoting to demands for love. Their synchronized 'why are we here?' is a funny tag.

jokes.text: Blow me a kiss. / Muah. Muah. / Caught it. I love you, Daddy! / I love you, Daddy! / I love you, too.
jokes.setup: After refusing to back off from destroying Tom, Saperstein reconciles with his children.
jokes.punchline: Saperstein demanding blown kisses from his adult children — 'Caught it' — and the children's enthusiastic compliance, is both heartwarming and aggressively weird.
jokes.explanation: The Saperstein family dynamics rendered perfectly: performative affection as the primary love language. 'Caught it' from Dr. Saperstein is a funny specific choice — he's very serious about catching blown kisses.

jokes.text: Hey, are you gonna be okay with Andy gone? / Yeah, it will be fine. / Are you gonna be okay with Ben still here? / April. / What? I don't trust him. I never have. He's after your money.
jokes.setup: Ben and April check in on each other after Andy's London news.
jokes.punchline: April deflects attention from her own feelings about Andy by accusing Ben of being a gold-digger, completely unprompted.
jokes.explanation: April's pivot from genuine vulnerability (Andy leaving) to unfounded suspicion of Ben is perfect April Ludgate emotional deflection. 'He's after your money' is both absurd (Leslie and Ben are government employees) and entirely consistent with April's general distrust.

jokes.text: I didn't want all the slugs gone. / I wanted most of them gone. / So sorry. Well, we'll put one slug back.
jokes.setup: Leslie resolves the slug problem using knowledge from her London trip.
jokes.punchline: The constituent clarifies she only wanted MOST slugs gone — not all. Leslie immediately offers to put one slug back. The callback to the original absurd demand ('but not too happy') escalates to its logical conclusion.
jokes.explanation: The callback payoff to the slug subplot is very satisfying. 'Well, we'll put one slug back' — Leslie's immediate willingness to re-slug someone's yard — is absurdist but completely in character. It also closes a three-act structure: complaint → journey → resolution (one slug). Good callback construction.

jokes.text: These were a gift from your British friend, Lord Edgar Covington. He was very impressed with you two. He sounded rich on the phone. I think he was calling me from a helicopter. / Could be. He owns two.
jokes.setup: The office receives a gift from Lord Covington.
jokes.punchline: 'He sounded rich on the phone. I think he was calling me from a helicopter.' The specificity of helicopter-phone as indicator of wealth, confirmed by Ben: 'He owns two.'
jokes.explanation: A light and functional joke. The specific detail of helicopter-as-phone-location is a good image. Ben's casual confirmation ('he owns two') is a nice character note about how quickly Ben has normalized Covington's extreme wealth.

jokes.text: Eddie? / Uh-oh. SpaghettiOs... / Oh, don't worry. I'm sure he'll adjust. / No. I named that dog 'SpaghettiOs,' and he just pooped in your briefcase.
jokes.setup: April and Ben read Andy's email about getting lost in London.
jokes.punchline: April clarifies she wasn't worried about Andy adjusting — she named the dog SpaghettiOs and it just pooped in Ben's briefcase. Complete non-sequitur that reframes her previous silence.
jokes.explanation: The misdirect is excellent — we think April is worried about Andy, then it turns out she's referring to a dog named SpaghettiOs who is actively defecating in Ben's briefcase. The name 'SpaghettiOs' is a perfect April-level non-name for a dog. Ben's 'Okay' in response is the ideal straight-man reaction.

jokes.text: Come on, Sugarbutt. / Oh. Which one's Sugarbutt? / That's you. Come on. We've got a board meeting. Sugarbutt.
jokes.setup: April calls for 'Sugarbutt' after the SpaghettiOs revelation.
jokes.punchline: Ben assumes 'Sugarbutt' is another dog. April clarifies it's Ben. April has named Ben 'Sugarbutt' for the board meeting.
jokes.explanation: A perfect April joke. The reveal that April has named BEN 'Sugarbutt' — not a dog — and is calling him that for a board meeting is simultaneously absurd and perfectly in character. The final 'Sugarbutt.' at the end, used as an earnest summons, is the best possible button. 'Wildly inappropriate' from Ben is the perfect reaction. Very quotable.

jokes.text: Wildly inappropriate.
jokes.setup: April has just named Ben 'Sugarbutt' and is calling him that for a board meeting.
jokes.punchline: Ben's understated 'wildly inappropriate' is the perfect reaction — not angry, not amused, just registering the precise level of violation.
jokes.explanation: Two words, maximum effect. Ben's register — not outrage, not laughter, just precise calibration of inappropriateness — is perfect. The economy score is a 10: you could not do this in fewer words.

jokes.text: I thought I was a better-looking version of Zuckerberg. It turns out I'm the better-looking version of the Winklevoss twins.
jokes.setup: Tom is despairing about losing to Saperstein.
jokes.punchline: Tom's self-assessment — from 'better-looking Zuckerberg' (winner) to 'better-looking Winklevoss twins' (people who got beaten by Zuckerberg) — is a great self-deprecating use of the Social Network analogy.
jokes.explanation: An excellent analogy that works on multiple levels: (1) it's character-specific (Tom constantly compares himself to celebrities), (2) the Facebook parallel to Rent A Swag vs. the knockoff is apt, (3) 'the better-looking version of the Winklevoss twins' is both a self-compliment and a self-insult simultaneously. Good construction.

jokes.text: First of all, unbelievable analogy. / Second of all, what are you talking about, man? / When Babyface was your age, he hadn't even signed Toni Braxton yet. Let alone Usher.
jokes.setup: Jean-Ralphio is trying to inspire Tom.
jokes.punchline: Jean-Ralphio's motivational speech uses Babyface (the R&B producer) as the model for entrepreneurial success — 'when Babyface was your age, he hadn't even signed Toni Braxton yet' — completely specific and completely absurd.
jokes.explanation: Jean-Ralphio using Babyface as his motivational touchstone is perfect character comedy — it's specific to his world (R&B), completely non-standard as a business inspiration, and delivered with absolute sincerity. 'Let alone Usher' is the perfect escalating button. The opening 'unbelievable analogy' — praising Tom for the Winklevoss comparison — is also good: Jean-Ralphio's values in one phrase. Very quotable.

jokes.text: Either my best friend emerges triumphant, or my dad beats you and I get all that money when he dies.
jokes.setup: Jean-Ralphio has just inspired Tom to keep fighting.
jokes.punchline: Jean-Ralphio's admission that a win for Tom's enemy is also fine because he inherits the money is a perfect Jean-Ralphio self-interest reveal — affection and mercenary calculation coexisting without tension.
jokes.explanation: Jean-Ralphio's win-win: either Tom wins OR Jean-Ralphio inherits his dad's money. The casual admission of anticipating his father's death as option B — delivered with zero guilt — is a perfect character joke. The construction (emotional friendship speech → 'or my dad beats you and I get all that money') is an excellent tonal pivot.

jokes.text: You know what I just read? That right now, our baby is the size of a green olive. Isn't that wild? / It is. A green olive. / A little high in sodium.
jokes.setup: Chris and Ann discuss fetal development.
jokes.punchline: Chris's concern about the olive comparison: 'a little high in sodium.' He's critiquing the nutrition of the simile used to describe his unborn child.
jokes.explanation: Chris Traeger critiquing the sodium content of an olive-as-fetal-size metaphor is a perfect character joke. His health obsession is so deep it applies even to metaphors. 'A little high in sodium' is an unexpected angle on a universally familiar pregnancy milestone moment. Very quotable, very character-specific. One of the episode's best Chris Traeger jokes.

jokes.text: Every time Jerry looks at me, he's thinking about the milk in my boobs.
jokes.setup: Ann is discussing the privacy of her pregnancy after Jerry's oversharing.
jokes.punchline: Ann's specific concern about Jerry — not that he knows about the pregnancy, but that his gaze is now specifically calibrated to her boobs' milk content — is both funny and a reasonable paranoia given Jerry's earlier behavior.
jokes.explanation: A good callback to Jerry's creepy milk enthusiasm. Ann's specific articulation of her concern ('the milk in my boobs') is funny in its frankness. The callback to Jerry's 'rooting around for that nipple' behavior makes this land harder.

jokes.text: You know, Olive is kind of a cute name. If it's a girl. / I prefer Chick Pea. / Because it's lower in sodium? / Yes, exactly.
jokes.setup: The couple discusses potential baby names inspired by the olive comparison.
jokes.punchline: Chris prefers 'Chick Pea' as a name because it's lower in sodium — the callback to his sodium concern about the olive, now applied to baby naming. His 'yes, exactly' confirms this is genuinely his reasoning.
jokes.explanation: A beautiful callback construction. The olive sodium joke earlier now pays off: Chris would literally name his child based on sodium content. 'Yes, exactly' — his complete confirmation that this is genuine — is the perfect button. Excellent structure: the setup four minutes earlier makes this callback land with real precision. Very quotable and earns the callback bonus.

jokes.text: I feel like you're getting sad about how stupid and lame people are. And that is my job, not yours.
jokes.setup: Ron notices Leslie is demoralized by the slug lady's ingratitude.
jokes.punchline: Ron's job description — being sad about how stupid and lame people are — is both funny and a perfect summary of his character. His territorial claim over this emotional register is very Ron.
jokes.explanation: Ron claiming exclusive rights to disappointment in humanity is a perfect character beat. The framing — 'that is my job, not yours' — positions his cynicism as a professional role he occupies so others don't have to. It's also a sweet gesture: he's protecting Leslie's optimism while owning his own pessimism. Beautiful economy and character integration.

jokes.text: But if you hug me afterwards, I swear to God, I'll scream and pull my hair out and maybe punch you in the face.
jokes.setup: Ron is about to read a touching letter about Leslie and gives her a warning.
jokes.punchline: Ron's escalating anti-hug threat — scream, pull hair out, 'maybe punch you in the face' — reveals both his discomfort with emotional expression and the depth of the feeling he's about to share.
jokes.explanation: The escalation of anti-hug violence is funny, but what makes this land is the subtext: Ron is about to do something deeply kind and emotional, and he's pre-emptively defending himself. His discomfort with his own generosity is the real joke. The specific escalation to 'maybe punch you in the face' — the 'maybe' suggests even he's not sure he'd go that far — is a great touch.

jokes.text: Sincerely, Satan.
jokes.setup: Ron has been reading a beautiful, heartfelt letter about Leslie — clearly written by someone who loves her deeply.
jokes.punchline: The letter is signed 'Sincerely, Satan' — Ron's nom de plume, confirming that this deeply loving letter came from him. The contrast between the tenderness of the letter and 'Satan' as the signature is the entire joke.
jokes.explanation: The episode's best joke and one of the finest Ron Swanson moments in the series. The structure is perfect: Ron reads an increasingly warm, vulnerable, specific letter about Leslie — a letter that reveals exactly how much he loves her — and then destroys/confirms his persona in two words: 'Sincerely, Satan.' It works on every level: (1) Ron would never admit he wrote such a thing, so the pseudonym is protection; (2) 'Satan' captures his self-image as a curmudgeon who hates emotions; (3) the juxtaposition with the letter's tenderness is a comedic and emotional gut-punch; (4) it's a perfect callback to his anti-hug warning. This is character comedy at its best — the joke IS the character, and the joke makes us love the character more, not less. Economy is perfect. Structure is outstanding. Comparable to or exceeding the calibration anchor.

jokes.text: You're getting hugged right now. / No. I told you not to. / I'm giving you a hug. / No. Stay away. No.
jokes.setup: Ron has just revealed the tender letter and warned against hugging.
jokes.punchline: Leslie immediately violates the anti-hug rule. Ron's resistance — 'No. Stay away. No.' — is a protest that is clearly not entirely sincere.
jokes.explanation: The payoff to Ron's anti-hug warning. His resistance — 'no, no, stay away, no' — while clearly not using full Ron Swanson force to prevent it, is a perfect emotional button to the scene. The callback structure is tight: warning → violation → theatrical protest. The physical comedy is implied and funny.

jokes.text: All my life, I have avoided Europe and its multitudes of terribleness. But it turns out, much to my surprise, there is actually one place in Europe that is worth seeing.
jokes.setup: Ron narrates his journey through Europe, maintaining his anti-European stance.
jokes.punchline: The setup promises a Ron Swanson location reveal — the one exception to European terribleness.
jokes.explanation: 'Its multitudes of terribleness' is a great Ron phrase. The setup for the Scotch whiskey reveal is well-constructed — it's exactly the one exception Ron would choose, and the reveal is deeply satisfying. Good character integration throughout.

jokes.text: These tiny islands off the coast of Scotland, where God's chosen elixirs are distilled, barreled, and prepared for consumption. This is worth the trip.
jokes.setup: Ron has revealed the one place in Europe worth visiting.
jokes.punchline: Scotch whiskey distilleries. 'God's chosen elixirs' — Ron's genuine theological reverence for whiskey. 'This is worth the trip' — from London to Scotland to see whiskey. His priorities perfectly expressed.
jokes.explanation: 'God's chosen elixirs' applied to Scotch whiskey is a perfect Ron Swanson phrase — genuinely theological in his commitment. The payoff to the 'one place worth seeing' setup being a distillery is exactly right. Very quotable and deeply character-specific.

jokes.text: I don't know what she thought I'd get out of that. [after reading Burns poem aloud]
jokes.setup: Leslie's wedding gift itinerary sent Ron to the Scottish cliffs to read Robert Burns poetry aloud.
jokes.punchline: After apparently reading the poem with some emotion (given the pause), Ron delivers 'I don't know what she thought I'd get out of that' — which is obviously false given his complete compliance and the silence that preceded it.
jokes.explanation: The best version of the Ron Swanson emotional denial joke. He just read a love poem aloud on a Scottish cliff and clearly got something from it — the pause is visible — but his response is complete denial. 'I don't know what she thought I'd get out of that' is pure Ron: denial as character armor, transparent to everyone including the audience. The rewatch bonus is for knowing what he actually felt.

jokes.text: Fine, Mongolia sounds terrifying. But the world is a very big place, and I've seen very little of it. Maybe we should travel more, expand our horizons.
jokes.setup: Leslie and Ben discuss how inspiring the episode's travel has been.
jokes.punchline: Leslie concedes Mongolia sounds terrifying (after spending the episode enamored with it) then immediately pivots to wanting to see more world.
jokes.explanation: A mild character moment. The Mongolia reversal is a small laugh. More plot-functional than comedic.

jokes.text: I got you something in London. A traditional barrister's wig. / Oh. / Wear it for me. / Yeah? / Mmm-hmm. / All right. [puts it on] / What's up? / No. Not sexy. / Failed experiment. Take it off.
jokes.setup: Leslie and Ben are having a sweet post-London moment. Leslie produces a gift.
jokes.punchline: The barrister's wig — Leslie's gift — is intended as a sexy thing. Ben puts it on. Leslie immediately rejects it: 'Not sexy. Failed experiment.' The anti-climax of the entire emotional episode ending on a failed sexy wig is a perfect button.
jokes.explanation: A great episode capper. After the emotional depth of the Ron/Leslie storyline, the episode ends with Ben in a barrister's wig being told 'not sexy' and 'failed experiment.' 'Failed experiment' — the clinical term for a non-working sexy wig — is a great Leslie Knope phrase. The anti-climax is perfect tonal management.

tmdb_overview: Leslie wins an award from an international Women in Government organization, and travels to London with Ben, Andy, April and Ron to accept it.
insight: London trip launches Season 6 with steady character comedy, 66 jokes sustaining an 80+ baseline.
